fact: Sequential access reads locations one after the other in sequence, and its example is magnetic tape
Random access means all locations can be accessed in constant time, and its example is RAM
Direct access works like locating a street, finding the vicinity or block first, and its example is the hard disk drive
Associative access holds the address and the content together, and its example is cache
Computer memory exhibits a number of characteristics: location, access methods, performance such as transfer rate, and capacity or size
Memory hierarchy is a structured arrangement of different storage types in a computer system, designed to optimize performance and cost
The memory trade-off is that faster access time means greater cost per bit, greater capacity means slower access, and smaller cost per bit means slower access
Design constraints on memory can be summed up by three questions: how much space, how fast is the access time, and how expensive
On capacity, if memory exists then applications will likely be developed to use it
Best performance is achieved when memory keeps up with the processor, so that as the processor executes instructions the memory minimizes pausing or waiting for instructions or operands
The cost of memory must be reasonable in relationship to other components
The way out of the memory dilemma is not to rely on a single memory but to employ a memory hierarchy, supplementing smaller, more expensive, faster memories with larger, cheaper, slower memories
As one goes down the memory hierarchy the cost per bit decreases, capacity increases and access time increases
As one goes down the memory hierarchy the frequency of access of memory by the processor decreases, which is very key to the performance of the CPU
The typical memory hierarchy from top to bottom is Level 1 Registers, Level 2 Cache Memory, Level 3 Main Memory (RAM), Level 4 Secondary Storage (SSD or HDD) and Level 5 Tertiary Storage
In the hierarchy table registers are fastest, highest in cost and smallest in capacity, while tertiary storage is slowest, lowest in cost and very large in capacity
In the hierarchy table cache memory is very fast, high in cost and small, while main memory is moderate in speed, medium in cost and medium in capacity
The lecture poses the in-class question: why do we not use only cache memory in a computer system?
We do not use only cache memory because cache is very expensive and has limited capacity
Spatial locality means that if we access a memory location, close by addresses will very likely be accessed, as in a loop operation
Temporal locality means that if we access a memory location, we will very likely access it again
Locality of reference is a consequence of using iterative loops and subroutines, because instructions and data will be accessed multiple times
In the two-level worked example, Level 1 contains 1000 words or bytes with an access time of 0.01 microseconds and Level 2 contains 100,000 words or bytes with an access time of 0.1 microseconds
In the two-level example, if the word is in L1 the processor accesses it directly in 0.01 microseconds, and if it is in L2 the word is first transferred to L1 and then accessed, costing 0.01 plus 0.1

In the two-level example H is the fraction of all memory accesses that are found in L1, T1 is the access time to L1 and T2 is the access time to L2, and the time for the processor to determine which level holds the word is ignored for simplicity
For high percentages of L1 access, the average total access time is much closer to that of L1 than that of L2
If 95% of memory accesses are found in L1, the average time to access a word is 0.95 times 0.01 plus 0.05 times 0.01 plus 0.1, which is 0.0095 plus 0.0055, giving 0.015 microseconds
The strategy to minimize accesses is to organize data across the hierarchy so that the percentage of accesses to lower levels is substantially less than that to upper levels

L2 holds all program instructions and data, data currently being used is held in L1, and eventually data in L1 is swapped out to L2 to make room for new data, so that on average most references are to data in L1
Processor registers are the fastest, smallest and most expensive type of memory
The cache stages data movement between registers and main memory, improves performance, and is not usually visible to the processor or to the programmer
Main memory is the principal internal memory system of the computer, and each of its locations has a unique address

Cache memory is designed to combine the memory access time of expensive, high-speed memory with the large memory size of less expensive, lower-speed memory, and it contains a copy of portions of main memory
Cache can be 1 to 2 MB while main memory can be up to 64 GB
A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits
A word is one or more complete rows of memory and a block is a collection of words, typically 2, 4 or 8
A memory size of 4 MB works out as 4 times 1024 times 1024 times 8, which is 33,554,432 bits, and 10 KB works out as 10 times 1024 times 8, which is 81,920 bits
When the processor attempts to read a word of memory a check is made to determine if the word is in the cache, and if it is, a cache hit, the word is delivered to the processor
On a cache miss the block of main memory that contains the word is read into the cache, and the cache then delivers the word to the processor
Because of the locality of reference principle, when a block of data is fetched into the cache it is likely that there will be future references to that same memory location
The cache concept is improved by introducing multiple levels of cache: L2 cache is slower and typically larger than L1 cache, and L3 cache is slower and typically larger than L2 cache
Main memory consists of 2 to the power n addressable words, each word having a unique n-bit address, and the memory consists of a number of fixed-length blocks of K words each
The number of main memory blocks is M equals 2 to the power n divided by K
Cache memory consists of m blocks called lines, each line contains K words, and each line also includes control bits
If a word in a block of memory is read, the whole block is transferred to a cache line
Because m is much less than M, the cache cannot permanently store a block, so it needs to identify the block stored, and that information is held in the tag field
In the cache read operation the processor generates the read address RA of the word to be read, and if the word is in the cache it is delivered to the processor
Otherwise the block containing that word is loaded into the cache and the word is delivered to the processor, these last two operations occurring in parallel

The cache connects to the processor via data, control and address lines, and the data and address lines also attach to data and address buffers, which attach to a system bus from which main memory is reached
When a cache hit occurs the data and address buffers are disabled, communication is only between processor and cache, and there is no system bus traffic
When a cache miss occurs the desired address is loaded onto the system bus and the data are returned through the data buffer to both the cache and the processor
There are two types of cache addresses: physical addresses, which are actual memory addresses, and logical addresses, which are virtual-memory addresses
Virtual memory performs mapping between the logical addresses used by a program and physical addresses, and its main idea is to disregard the amount of main memory available
A virtual cache stores data using logical addresses, so the processor accesses the cache directly without going through the MMU
The advantage of a virtual cache is faster access speed, since the cache can respond without the need for an MMU address translation

The disadvantage of a virtual cache is that the same virtual address in two different applications refers to two different physical addresses, so the cache must be flushed at each application context switch, or extra bits must be added to each cache line to identify which virtual address space the address refers to

Cache size should be small enough that the overall average cost per bit is close to that of main memory alone, and large enough that the overall average access time is close to that of the cache alone
The larger the cache the more complex the addressing logic, with the result that large caches tend to be slightly slower than small ones, and available chip and board area also limits cache size
